Yes. Every all- $P$  unit square of  $H$  can always be removed. In fact, there is a stronger local statement:Theorem. Under the hypotheses in the question, there is a feasible endpoint-promotion bundle supported on  $M|_H$  that leaves at most one matching edge in  $H$ . Consequently, at most two vertices of  $H$  remain in  $P$ , and all  $w-1$  all- $P$  unit squares disappear.Single terminality is unnecessary.Here a  $P$ -square means a unit face whose four vertices belong to  $P$ , consistently with the  $w-1$  squares in your stated interior-color fact.The distinction from removing every endpoint matters: complete endpoint removal can fail, even in a single-terminal configuration. I give an explicit example after the proof, showing that the one-edge remainder in the theorem is sometimes necessary.1. Exterior supports and the only difficult caseWrite
$$H=\{0,1\}\times\{0,\ldots,w-1\}.$$
For  $z\in H$ , let  $s(z)$  be the number of its occupied neighbors outside  $H$ .Because  $H$  is a complete connected component of the graph induced by  $P$ , every occupied exterior neighbor of  $H$  belongs to  $T$ . Such a vertex already has an occupied neighbor in  $H$ , so feasibility prohibits any additional occupied neighbor.For the perpendicular supports, put
$$\tau_0(j)=\mathbf 1_{\{(-1,j)\in T\}},
\qquad
\tau_1(j)=\mathbf 1_{\{(2,j)\in T\}}.$$
A site outside the finite ambient grid has indicator zero. The preceding observation gives
$$\tau_r(j)+\tau_r(j+1)\le 1
\qquad
(r\in\{0,1\},\ 0\le j<w-1).
\tag{1}$$
Likewise, the two lateral support sites immediately left of  $H$  cannot both belong to  $T$ , and neither can the two immediately right of  $H$ .Only corners of  $H$  can have two exterior supports. Call such a corner doubly supported. We obtain two useful consequences:There is at most one doubly supported corner at each end of  $H$ .If an end has a doubly supported corner, the other corner at that end has no lateral support.The second point follows because a doubly supported corner uses its lateral support, which is adjacent to the other lateral support site.If all doubly supported corners have the same checkerboard color, promote the other checkerboard color on every matching edge of  $H$ . This is feasible: the promoted vertices have no occupied neighbors inside  $H$ , and each has at most one exterior support. If there are no doubly supported corners, either color works.Thus the only remaining case is:there are two doubly supported corners;they lie at opposite ends;they have opposite checkerboard colors.Let  $C$  be the color that avoids the left doubly supported corner, and let  $D$  be the other color. Thus  $D$  avoids the right doubly supported corner.We will promote color  $C$  on the left and color  $D$  on the right, retaining one carefully chosen domino between them.2. Decompose the actual matching into blocksEvery perfect matching of a two-row rectangle decomposes, from left to right, into blocks of two possible types:Block typeColumns occupiedMatching edges $V$ OneOne vertical domino $HH$ TwoBoth horizontal dominoes across those columnsTo prove this, inspect the leftmost remaining column. Either its two vertices are matched vertically, giving a  $V$  block, or its top vertex is matched horizontally to the next column. In the latter case, its bottom vertex must also be matched horizontally to the next column, giving an  $HH$  block. Remove that block and repeat.In particular, no matching edge crosses between these blocks. This decomposition accommodates arbitrary mixtures of horizontal and vertical dominoes, including matching edges that cross the boundary of the strict interior in the question.Write the blocks as
$$B_1,\ldots,B_m,$$
where  $B_i$  occupies columns
$$[a_i,b_i].$$
3. A block with two blank support guards always existsFor a checkerboard color  $E\in\{C,D\}$ , let  $v_E(j)$  denote the unique vertex of color  $E$  in column  $j$ . Write  $\tau(v)$  for the perpendicular support indicator of a vertex  $v\in H$ .For each block define
$$L_i=
\begin{cases}
0,&a_i=0,\\
\tau\bigl(v_C(a_i-1)\bigr),&a_i>0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
R_i=
\begin{cases}
0,&b_i=w-1,\\
\tau\bigl(v_D(b_i+1)\bigr),&b_i<w-1.
\end{cases}
\tag{2}$$
These are the perpendicular support indicators at the vertices that would be promoted immediately to the left and right of the block under our chosen colors.There is a small boundary point to check here. If the left guard lies in column  $0$ , it has color  $C$ , so it is the corner opposite the left doubly supported corner. Its lateral support is therefore blank. Similarly, if the right guard lies in column  $w-1$ , its lateral support is blank. All other guard vertices are noncorners.Consequently,
$$L_i=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{the existing left guard has no occupied exterior neighbor},
\tag{3}$$
and the analogous statement holds for  $R_i=0$ .Now consider consecutive blocks. Since
$$a_{i+1}=b_i+1,$$
the vertices tested by  $R_i$  and  $L_{i+1}$  are
$$v_D(b_i+1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
v_C(b_i).$$
They lie in the same row at consecutive columns: changing column changes checkerboard color. Their perpendicular support sites are therefore adjacent. By (1),
$$R_i+L_{i+1}\le1.
\tag{4}$$
Also,
$$L_1=0,\qquad R_m=0.
\tag{5}$$
Take the first block  $B_k$  for which  $R_k=0$ . Such a block exists by (5). If  $k=1$ , then  $L_k=0$ . If  $k>1$ , minimality gives  $R_{k-1}=1$ , so (4) again gives  $L_k=0$ .We have therefore found a block satisfying
$$\boxed{L_k=R_k=0.}
\tag{6}$$
This is the existence argument that handles occupied guards: a fixed proposed block need not work, but some block of the actual matching must work.4. Construct the bundleFix the block  $B_k=[a,b]$  from (6).On every matching edge strictly left of  $B_k$ , promote its  $C$ -colored endpoint.On every matching edge strictly right of  $B_k$ , promote its  $D$ -colored endpoint.It remains to specify what happens inside  $B_k$ .Before checking the two cases, observe that every original  $T$ -vertex automatically remains feasible. If  $V$  is the set of endpoints made blank, then the new occupied set is exactly
$$A'=A\setminus V.
\tag{7}$$
Promotion changes an already occupied endpoint into a  $T$ -vertex; it creates no newly occupied site. Thus occupied degrees of original  $T$ -vertices cannot increase.We need only check the newly promoted vertices.Case A:  $B_k$  is a vertical blockLeave its vertical matching edge unchanged.Within each side of the retained column, the promoted vertices form one checkerboard color. Their neighbors within that side are blank.The only promoted vertices that can have occupied neighbors inside  $H$  are the two immediate guards from (2). Each existing guard has exactly one such neighbor, an endpoint of the retained vertical domino. By (3) and (6), it has no exterior occupied neighbor.Every other promoted vertex has no occupied neighbor inside  $H$  and at most one exterior support. Neither doubly supported corner is promoted: it is either avoided by the color used at its end or belongs to the retained column.Hence the resulting pair is feasible.Case B:  $B_k$  is a horizontal blockNow  $b=a+1$ , and the block contains two horizontal matching edges.Let  $q$  be the row whose vertex in column  $a$  has color  $D$ . The colors in this row across the block are therefore
$$D,\ C.$$
Retain the horizontal matching edge in row  $q$ .The left  $C$ -guard in column  $a-1$ , when present, lies in row  $q$ . The right  $D$ -guard in column  $a+2$ , when present, also lies in row  $q$ .Let  $p$  be the other row. Its two vertices in the block have colors
$$C,\ D.$$
By (1), at least one of
$$\tau_p(a),\qquad \tau_p(a+1)$$
is zero. Promote an endpoint of the row- $p$  horizontal domino with zero perpendicular support, and make its mate blank.We check this central promoted vertex first.Its vertical neighbor belongs to the retained row- $q$  domino, so it has one occupied neighbor inside the block.Its matching partner is blank.Its horizontal neighbor outside the block, if present, is blank. On either side, the promoted outside guard lies in row  $q$ , not row  $p$ .Its perpendicular exterior support is blank by construction.If this promoted vertex is at an end of  $H$ , its lateral support is also blank. Indeed:If  $a=0$ , the row- $q$  vertex at column  $a$  has color  $D$ , so it is the left doubly supported corner.If  $a+1=w-1$ , the row- $q$  vertex at column  $a+1$  has color  $C$ , so it is the right doubly supported corner.At either end, the other row has no lateral support. Thus the central promoted vertex has occupied degree exactly one.The two outside guards, when present, each meet one endpoint of the retained domino and have no exterior occupied neighbor by (3) and (6). Every other promoted vertex has no occupied neighbor inside  $H$  and at most one exterior support.The resulting pair is therefore feasible in this case too.5. All  $P$ -squares disappearIn either construction in the difficult case, exactly one matching edge of  $H$  is retained. All other  $w-1$  matching edges are promoted. Since  $w\ge2$ , the bundle is nonempty.Thus
$$|P'\cap H|=2,$$
which makes an all- $P$  unit square in  $H$  impossible.The objective is preserved explicitly:
$$|T'|=|T|+(w-1),
\qquad
|M'|=|M|-(w-1),$$
and hence
$$|T'|+|M'|=|T|+|M|.$$
In the earlier whole-color case, all  $w$  matching edges are promoted instead.This proves the theorem. No part of the argument used single terminality. It uses the stipulated rule that feasibility is the only condition on the resulting pair.6. One residual domino can genuinely be necessaryHere is a feasible, single-terminal example in which removing every endpoint of  $H$  is impossible.Take
$$H=\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2\},$$
with the three vertical matching edges
$$M=\bigl\{\{(0,j),(1,j)\}:j=0,1,2\bigr\}.$$
Use the finite ambient rectangle
$$\{-1,0,1,2\}\times\{-1,0,1,2,3\},$$
and set
$$T=
\{(-1,0),(-1,2),(2,0),(2,2),(0,-1),(1,3)\}.
\tag{8}$$
All other sites outside  $H$  are blank.Verification of the original configurationThe six vertices in (8) are pairwise nonadjacent, and each has exactly one occupied neighbor, lying in  $H$ . Thus the pair is feasible, and  $H$  is its complete endpoint component.The occupied degrees of the endpoints are:EndpointsOccupied degreeUpper-left  $(0,0)$ , lower-right  $(1,2)$  $4$ Lower-left  $(1,0)$ , upper-right  $(0,2)$  $3$ Both middle-column vertices $3$ So the configuration is single-terminal.Why complete endpoint removal is impossibleA bundle removing every endpoint of  $H$  would have to select all three vertical matching edges.The doubly supported upper-left corner  $(0,0)$  cannot be promoted, because its two exterior  $T$ -neighbors remain occupied. Therefore the left domino must promote  $(1,0)$ .Similarly, the doubly supported lower-right corner  $(1,2)$  cannot be promoted, so the right domino must promote  $(0,2)$ .But:The promoted vertex  $(1,0)$  already has its exterior support  $(2,0)$ . It therefore forces  $(1,1)$  to be blank.The promoted vertex  $(0,2)$  already has its exterior support  $(-1,2)$ . It therefore forces  $(0,1)$  to be blank.Both endpoints of the middle matching edge would have to be blank. An endpoint-promotion orientation must retain one of them as  $T$ , which is a contradiction.Nevertheless, both  $P$ -squares can be removedSelect only the vertical matching edges in columns  $0$  and  $1$ , with orientations
$$(u_0,v_0)=((1,0),(0,0)),
\qquad
(u_1,v_1)=((0,1),(1,1)).$$
Retain the rightmost vertical matching edge.The new vertex  $(1,0)$  has only its exterior support occupied. The new vertex  $(0,1)$  has only the retained endpoint  $(0,2)$  occupied. Original  $T$ -vertices remain feasible by (7).Both unit  $P$ -squares disappear, while exactly one domino remains. Thus the theorem’s bound of one residual matching edge is sharp.7. Relation to a global coloring inequalityThe precise pure-component extension asked here is therefore true: arbitrary matching escape across the strict interior and occupied boundary guards do not obstruct removal of all  $P$ -squares.The example above refutes the stronger demand to remove every endpoint. It does not refute square removal or supply a counterexample to a global coloring inequality.Conversely, the theorem establishes a local transformation preserving  $|T|+|M|$ . A global numerical coloring bound would require its own counting argument. No universal  $5/6$  improvement follows from this local result alone.
